_comment: A/BOT's script. Not a live model — scripted content keeps the site static, fast and free (plan §6). Every line here is subject to tone rule §4: jokes land on hype, on jargon, or on A/BOT itself, never on the Organization, its officials or any Member State.

intro.name: A/BOT
intro.symbolJoke: Yes, my name is formatted like a General Assembly document symbol. No, I do not have a resolution number. I am working on it.
intro.greeting: Hello! I explain AI governance through Star Wars, Asimov and the occasional dragon. Pick a mode below, or tap any underlined term in the timeline and I will meet you there.
capabilities: Glossary — tap any underlined word for a plain-language definition and an analogy
Quests — short guided routes through the timeline for five common situations
Real AI — how to go ask an actual model about any of this

glossary.short: Software that performs tasks we used to think needed a human — recognising images, writing text, making predictions. The UN has no single agreed definition, which is itself a live negotiating issue.
glossary.analogy: Like the word "vehicle". Useful until someone asks whether it covers a skateboard.

glossary.short: AI that produces new text, images, audio or code rather than just classifying things. ChatGPT is the example that made the term a household word in 2023.
glossary.analogy: The difference between a critic who reviews films and a studio that makes them.

glossary.short: A model trained on enormous amounts of text to predict what comes next, which turns out to be enough to draft, summarise and translate. The engine under most generative AI you have used.
glossary.analogy: Autocomplete that read the whole library. Astonishingly capable, occasionally very confidently wrong.

glossary.short: The largest and most capable models at any given moment — the ones whose behaviour is least well understood. The term shifts every year, on purpose.
glossary.analogy: "Frontier" in the old cartographers' sense: the bit of the map where the labels run out.

glossary.short: Making a system actually pursue what its operators intend, including in situations nobody wrote down. Distinct from capability — a more powerful model is not automatically a better-behaved one.
glossary.analogy: Rick's portal gun is impressive. Rick using it responsibly is the hard part.

glossary.short: The processing power used to train and run models, and one of the sharpest inequalities in AI. Access to it is now a development and governance question, not just a procurement one.
glossary.analogy: Everyone can read the recipe. Not everyone has the kitchen.

glossary.short: Making different countries' AI rules work together well enough that a system built under one can be assessed under another. Not the same as identical rules everywhere.
glossary.analogy: Plug adapters. Nobody agrees on the socket, so we standardise the adapter.

glossary.short: Practical help — skills, infrastructure, data, financing, institutions — so that every country can shape and use AI rather than only receive it. A distinct pillar of UN AI work since A/RES/78/311.
glossary.analogy: Not handing someone a telescope. Making sure there is an observatory, and someone trained to run it.

glossary.short: A text that sets standards States agree to be guided by. It is not a treaty and does not bind, but it shapes national law, procurement and institutional practice.
glossary.analogy: Asimov's Three Laws, except negotiated by 193 governments and considerably longer.

glossary.short: Adoption without anyone calling for a vote. It signals that no delegation objected strongly enough to force one — which is a meaningful political fact about a text.
glossary.analogy: Getting every house to sign the same document. The Global Digital Compact is basically a peace treaty everyone actually signed.

glossary.short: A formal count where each delegation's position is recorded and published. Used when a text is significant enough that States want their position on the record.
glossary.analogy: The show of hands, minuted, forever.

glossary.short: A formal decision of a UN organ. General Assembly resolutions are not legally binding, but they create mandates, establish bodies and set the agenda for years.
glossary.analogy: Not a law. More like a very well-attended decision about what everyone is going to work on next.

glossary.short: The identifier on every UN document — A/RES/79/325, S/PV.10005. The letter is the organ, the numbers are the session and the sequence. Cite it and anyone can find the text in seconds.
glossary.analogy: A postcode for paperwork. Once you can read them, the whole system opens up.

glossary.short: A formal sitting of the full General Assembly, numbered within its session. The place a resolution is actually adopted.
glossary.analogy: The whole school assembly, not the committee that drafted the notice.

glossary.short: One of the 193 countries that make up the UN's membership. In the General Assembly each has one vote, regardless of size.
glossary.analogy: One country, one vote — the rare room where that is literally true.

glossary.short: A country's diplomatic office at the UN, in New York or Geneva. Some have dozens of diplomats; some have three, covering everything.
glossary.analogy: An embassy, except accredited to an organisation instead of a country.

glossary.short: The UN's international civil service — the staff who service meetings, write reports and implement mandates. Distinct from the Member States who decide them.
glossary.analogy: The people who run the building, as opposed to the people who decide what happens in it.

glossary.short: The UN's universal body: all 193 Member States, one vote each. It creates mandates, establishes bodies and adopts resolutions — including both AI mechanisms established in 2025.
glossary.analogy: The one meeting everybody is invited to, and the only one where everyone counts equally.

glossary.short: The UN organ responsible for international peace and security, with 15 members and binding decision-making power. It first discussed AI in July 2023.
glossary.analogy: The room where decisions carry legal weight. Fifteen seats, and a very long agenda.

glossary.short: The digital and AI commitments agreed by all 193 Member States in September 2024 as Annex I to the Pact for the Future. The first truly universal AI-governance commitments.
glossary.analogy: The moment the whole map agreed on a legend.

glossary.short: 40 independent experts appointed by the General Assembly in February 2026 to produce evidence-based assessments of AI. Members serve in their personal capacity, and the mandate is non-military.
glossary.analogy: The Jedi Council of AI: convened for wisdom, advisory by design, no lightsabers, sadly.

glossary.short: The recurring universal forum where all Member States and stakeholders discuss AI governance. It met for the first time in Geneva in July 2026 and closes with a co-chairs' summary rather than a negotiated text.
glossary.analogy: A standing invitation rather than a one-off summit — which is the point.

glossary.short: The rules that define what a body does, who sits on it, how it is chosen and what it must report. Deeply unglamorous, and the thing that determines whether a mechanism actually works.
glossary.analogy: The character sheet. Written before anyone rolls a die, and it decides what you can do all campaign.

glossary.short: Weapons that can select and engage targets without further human intervention. There is no agreed definition, which is a substantive part of the negotiation rather than a technicality.
glossary.analogy: Science fiction spent decades on this question. The difference is that here the room is real, the lawyers are real, and so are the stakes.

glossary.short: Keeping a person genuinely able to understand, intervene in and be accountable for what a system does. "Genuinely" is doing enormous work in that sentence.
glossary.analogy: A co-pilot who is actually awake, rather than a co-pilot listed on the roster.

glossary.short: Identifying, preventing and accounting for the human-rights harms your activity might cause — including when you procure or deploy someone else's AI system.
glossary.analogy: Checking the brakes before you sell the car, not after.

glossary.short: The gap between countries that can build, buy and govern AI and those that cannot — spanning connectivity, compute, data, skills, language coverage and institutions.
glossary.analogy: Everyone is promised the same future. The delivery addresses differ.

glossary.short: Shared, open, interoperable systems for things like identity, payments and data exchange — public roads rather than private toll lanes.
glossary.analogy: Roads and post codes for the digital economy. Boring, and everything runs on it.

glossary.short: Models whose components are published so others can inspect, adapt and run them. A live governance question: openness aids scrutiny and access, and also lowers the barrier to misuse.
glossary.analogy: Publishing the recipe. Wonderful for cooks everywhere, and you no longer control who is in the kitchen.

glossary.short: The Secretary-General's push to modernise how the UN works, through data, digital, innovation, foresight and behavioural science — the "Quintet of Change".
glossary.analogy: Five upgrades installed while the system stays online. Anyone who has done a live migration is already wincing sympathetically.

facts: The 2023 AI for Good Summit held the world's first robot press conference. The robots were… diplomatic.
The phrase "artificial intelligence" appears in the UN Charter exactly zero times. In fairness, 1945 had other priorities.
A/RES/79/325 runs to detailed terms of reference for a 40-member panel. Somebody negotiated every one of those words, and I respect them enormously.
The Scientific Panel's 40 members were chosen from more than 2,600 applications from over 140 countries.
Document symbols are readable once you know the trick: organ, session, sequence. A/RES/79/325 is a General Assembly resolution, 79th session, number 325.
The Global Dialogue closes with a co-chairs' summary instead of a negotiated outcome — deliberately, so every delegation can speak on equal footing.
My name is formatted like a General Assembly document symbol. This was not an accident and I will not be taking questions.

realAI.heading: Want the real thing?
realAI.intro: I am a scripted droid — a JSON file with opinions. That keeps this site fast, free and entirely offline. But if you want to actually interrogate this material, go ask a real model. Paste any of these in:
prompts: Explain the Global Digital Compact like I'm a first-year diplomat. What did it actually commit States to?
What is the difference between the UN Scientific Panel on AI and the Global Dialogue on AI Governance? Who reports to whom?
I have to write a two-page briefing note on UN AI governance for a minister. Give me an outline with document symbols to cite.
Explain why a resolution adopted 'without a vote' is politically different from one adopted by recorded vote.
What are the hardest unsolved problems in global AI governance, and what has the UN put in place to address each one?
realAI.caveat: Then check what it tells you against the receipts on this page. Every node has them. That is the entire point of this site.
